qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 9: obsolete = lỗi thời, không còn được dùng nữa.

qs.q: Customer-service workers sometimes have to put ______ rude complaints from impatient callers.

qs.q: Minh deeply looks ______ his uncle, who started as an apprentice mechanic and now owns three car-repair centres.
qs.ex: Three-word phrasal verb: look up to = kính trọng, ngưỡng mộ.

qs.q: Even if you lack formal work experience, enthusiasm and a willingness to learn can make ______ it.
qs.ex: Three-word phrasal verb: make up for = bù đắp cho.

qs.q: Employers today value ______ skills—such as teamwork, problem-solving and adaptability—just as much as academic grades.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 9: soft skills = kỹ năng mềm.

qs.q: The marketing team came ______ a brilliant social-media campaign to promote local eco-products.
qs.ex: Three-word phrasal verb: come up with = nảy ra ý tưởng, sáng kiến.

qs.q: He worked so hard during his internship because he wanted to live ______ his mentor’s high expectations.
qs.ex: Three-word phrasal verb: live up to = xứng đáng với, đạt tới kỳ vọng của ai.

qs.q: If you have a strong passion for arts and crafts, you should go ______ a career in interior or fashion design.
qs.ex: Three-word phrasal verb: go in for = chọn theo đuổi, yêu thích tham gia.

qs.q: When automated machines replace routine factory tasks, technicians who can repair robots are highly ______.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 9: in demand = có nhu cầu tuyển dụng cao.

qs.q: I tried calling the company’s human-resources office three times this morning, but I couldn’t get ______ the manager.
qs.ex: Three-word phrasal verb: get through to somebody = liên lạc/nối máy được với ai.

qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation in Unit 9: Career Paths.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. To address this, schools and communities are now launching new career paths in the changing job market.
b. In the past, many people did not pay enough attention to exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation.
c. Today, however, both school-leavers and career advisers realise how important it is to build both technical expertise and soft skills.
d. As a result, everyone benefits when we work together to keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career.
e. These practical programmes help participants develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability in their daily lives.
qs.ex: Trình tự đoạn văn 5 câu: Thực trạng trước đây (b) → Nhận thức thay đổi ngày nay (c) → Giải pháp triển khai chương trình mới (a) → Tác dụng của các chương trình đó ('These practical programmes') (e) → Kết quả chung (d): b - c - a - e - d.

qs.q:
a. Linh: I’m preparing a poster about exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation for our English lesson tomorrow.
b. Minh: That sounds interesting! What main benefit are you highlighting on the poster?
c. Minh: Well done, Linh. I’m sure our classmates will learn a lot from your presentation!

**PERSPECTIVES ON CAREER PATHS**
In recent years, exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of school-leavers and career advisers recognise the importance of career paths, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**automated**</u> these practices into their daily routines in the changing job market. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to build both technical expertise and soft skills.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how career paths can keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should build both technical expertise and soft skills, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role in the changing job market. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation matters for the long-term future. Young people who see school-leavers and career advisers model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, career paths not only develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability today but also keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 9: Career Paths)

**MAKING CAREER PATHS PART OF DAILY LIFE**
Taking time to build both technical expertise and soft skills may seem ordinary at first glance, yet a growing body of research highlights its transformative power. Studies show that well-designed career paths help school-leavers and career advisers develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability. At the same time, these practices keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career and foster stronger cooperation in the changing job market.
Despite these clear advantages, participation in career paths has faced obstacles in recent years. Researchers report that <u>**they**</u> have been neglected in many busy communities due to modern time pressures. <u>**Tight timetables, heavy workloads and a lack of practical guidance can all prevent people from maintaining positive routines.**</u> Even when individuals want to improve, distractions often get in the way.
The encouraging news is that success does not require perfection from day one. Experts emphasise that building <u>**in demand**</u> habits is about steady progress rather than instant results. School-leavers and career advisers can start with simple steps in the changing job market, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**passion**</u> will grow stronger over time. What matters most is the commitment people bring to supporting one another every day.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 9: Career Paths)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of school-leavers and career advisers valued career paths, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market, teenagers were twice as likely to develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When school-leavers and career advisers work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 9: Career Paths)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
When people first decide to focus on exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced career paths are far more effective when built step by step, helping school-leavers and career advisers develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 9: Career Paths)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how career paths can develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising career paths independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 9: Career Paths to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 9: Career Paths)

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career.

Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising career paths independently. **THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When school-leavers and career advisers see their close friends willingly engage in career paths, they are far more likely to join in and develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 9: Career Paths)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
Why do many high school students agree that exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation is important, yet still find it difficult to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, school-leavers and career advisers can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on career paths. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 9: Career Paths report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, career paths stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 9: Career Paths)

qs.ex: reluctant = ngần ngại, miễn cưỡng (hesitant and unwilling).

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation. Rather than treating Unit 9: Career Paths as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on career paths. Through these authentic tasks, school-leavers and career advisers discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 9: Career Paths)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 9: CAREER PATHS**
Practising career paths is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps school-leavers and career advisers keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 9: Career Paths)

Practising career paths is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying exploring career paths, developing soft skills and adapting to automation have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to develop soft skills like critical thinking, teamwork and adaptability.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to build both technical expertise and soft skills in the changing job market this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps school-leavers and career advisers keep up with technological changes and choose a fulfilling career with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 9: Career Paths)
